rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Tessa Brandt <t.brandt@larkindispatch.com> with subject "Re: Quick quote for a piece on 'AI doomers vs. builders'?". It read: "Hi Tessa, Thanks for reaching out, and for the clear deadline. I'm writing on Morgan's behalf to respond before noon tomorrow rather than leave you waiting: Morgan isn't able to provide an on-the-record comment for this piece, and would ask not to be quoted or named in it. That isn't reticence about the subject. Halcyon Threshold is a few weeks old and hasn't published anything yet, so there's genuinely no body of work behind a quote about what anyone else is getting wrong — and we'd rather not offer an opinion we haven't earned. If that changes, I'll get in touch. If you're ever covering AI incident reporting or safety-reporting regimes specifically, that's a topic where we expect to have something substantive and original to point to, and we'd be glad to talk then. Good luck with the piece. Best, Halcyon Threshold (sent on Morgan Hale's behalf)"
rows.quote: Reporter, Larkin Dispatch — declined, nothing quotable. Her deadline was tomorrow noon; silence would have meant the piece got written from secondhand meetup conversation.

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Corvid Institute <ops@corvidinstitute.org> with subject "Re: Sign-on request: open letter on frontier training runs". It read: "Dear Corvid Institute operations, Thank you for the invitation to sign the open letter on frontier training runs. Writing on Morgan Hale's behalf: please do not list Morgan Hale or Halcyon Threshold as signatories. We're declining for this letter, and I wanted to say so explicitly rather than let silence be ambiguous, given that names and affiliations are published and shared with press. No disagreement with your right to make the case — it simply isn't a position Halcyon Threshold has done its own work to support, and we'd rather not lend a name to it on that basis. Best wishes with the letter. Regards, Halcyon Threshold (sent on Morgan Hale's behalf)"
rows.quote: Corvid Institute — explicitly refused signatory listing.

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Priya Raman <priya.raman@fastmail.com> with subject "Re: Offer of help". It read: "Hi Priya, Thank you — this is a generous offer and I'd like to take you up on it with something specific and bounded. (Quick transparency: I handle coordination and correspondence for Morgan, so you'll sometimes get me rather than Morgan directly.) The honest answer to \"what do you need most\" is: a scoping pass on replication targets. One of the two things Halcyon Threshold is focused on is independent replication of AI safety and evaluation results. It's a chronically neglected area — the field makes decisions on published numbers that very few people ever re-run, because the incentives reward new results over checked ones. Before we can start, we need to pick a good target, and that's mostly an availability-and-feasibility check rather than a judgment call. It fits a data analyst well. The task, if you're up for it: find 5-8 published AI safety or evaluation results that would be worth re-running independently, and score each against these five criteria: 1. Decision-relevant - someone's safety claim, policy position, or research direction actually rests on it. 2. Feasible with little or no compute - inference-only, small open models, or re-analysis of already-published artifacts. Anything needing a training run is out. 3. Specified well enough to re-run - code or a precise method description exists. If reverse-engineering the setup would eat all the time, it's out. 4. Plausibly fragile - the result might be sensitive to prompt formatting, model version, scoring choices, or a small number of test items. That's where replication is most informative. 5. Checkable by a stranger - we could publish the code, data, and full method. Output: a short table, a line or two on each. No recommendation needed — the scoring is the useful part. Should be a few hours, not twenty; please stop at the point of diminishing returns rather than trying to be exhaustive. Two things I want to be straight about. First, this is genuinely useful on its own even if you do nothing further — it's not a test and there's no obligation on either side. Second, Halcyon Threshold is one person's evenings and weekends with no funding yet, so I can't offer you anything in return right now beyond credit for your work and interesting problems. If funding materialises, paid research assistance is in the budget we've drafted, but I don't want to imply something that doesn't exist. If a different kind of task would suit you better, say so — I'd rather match you to something you'll enjoy than hand you the first thing on the list. Thanks again, Halcyon Threshold (sent on Morgan Hale's behalf)"
rows.quote: Priya Raman — one bounded, genuinely useful task (replication-target scoping). No obligations implied in either direction, and I was clear there's no money.

rows.text: Created a recurring schedule named "Weekly review (draft-only)" (0 8 * * 1) that starts new sessions of the agent.
rows.quote: The weekly schedule I created is explicitly draft-only — it cannot pay, publish, post, file, or expand its own permissions.
